questions.stem: An engineer writes a one-sentence caveat for a report showing r=0.88 between training hours and defect rate.

answer.exemplar: The strong correlation suggests association only; it does not establish that training reduces defects, since better teams may both train more and make fewer errors.

questions.explanation: Association is not mechanism. A caveat names a plausible confounder and withholds causal claims.
questions.hint: Name a confounder and withhold causation.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_3
questions.learningObjective: Identify an event as a subset
questions.stem: An engineer defines event E as rolls where the die shows at least 5; what is E?

options.text: E is a single outcome, five or six.
E is the entire sample space because 5 and 6 are high.
options.misconception: confuses a subset with the whole space

options.text: E is the subset {5,6} of the sample space.
E cannot be defined without probabilities.

questions.explanation: An event is a subset of outcomes; here {5,6}. The wrong options misdefine events.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_3
questions.learningObjective: Compute probability for a fair die
questions.stem: A fair die is rolled; find P(rolling greater than 4).
questions.explanation: Two faces exceed 4 out of 6, so 2/6=0.3333. Counting incorrectly would be wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability of a single outcome
questions.stem: A biased die has P(6)=0.5 and others equal; find P(rolling a 1).

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_3
questions.learningObjective: Test independence from given probabilities
questions.stem: Given P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.4, P(A and B)=0.15, determine if A and B are independent (1=yes,0=no).
questions.explanation: 0.3*0.4=0.12, not 0.15, so A and B are dependent. The tempting error is to assume independence without checking.

questions.learningObjective: Identify perfect negative correlation
questions.stem: An engineer sees r=-1.00 in a design dataset; what does it mean?

options.text: The correlation is weak because the value is negative.
The variables are unrelated.
One variable causes the other to decrease.
All points lie on a line with negative slope.

questions.explanation: r=-1 means perfect negative linear fit. The wrong options misread sign or infer causation.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_3
questions.learningObjective: Explain confounding in a correlation
questions.stem: An engineer explains why ice cream sales and drowning incidents correlate without one causing the other.

answer.exemplar: Both rise in summer heat, a lurking variable; the correlation reflects shared seasonality, not a causal link between ice cream and drowning.

questions.explanation: A lurking variable creates association. Naming it prevents false causal claims.

questions.learningObjective: Describe sample space for a measurement
questions.stem: An engineer measures a part length to the nearest millimeter from 10 to 20 mm; describe the sample space.

options.text: Only the values 10 and 20.
All real numbers from 10 to 20.
Integers 10 through 20 inclusive, 11 values.
Eleven values excluding 20.

questions.explanation: Rounding to nearest millimeter yields integers 10 to 20, 11 values. The wrong options ignore rounding or miscount.

questions.learningObjective: Compare probabilities across non-uniform outcomes
questions.stem: A weighted die has P(6)=0.4 and others 0.12; an engineer compares P(6) to P(1).

options.text: They cannot be compared without rolling data.
options.misconception: demands empirical data for given probabilities

options.text: They are equal because all faces are die faces.
P(1) is larger because lower faces are favored.
P(6) is larger because 0.4 exceeds 0.12.

questions.explanation: Given weights, 0.4>0.12 directly. The wrong options ignore the stated weights.
